questions.question: Describe a person who has helped you learn something important.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about my high school physics teacher, Mr Zhang, who helped me learn how to deal with failure. I first met him in my second year of high school, when I moved into his class. At that time I was a very anxious student, and whenever I got a bad mark I would give up on the subject completely. After one exam where I scored really low, he asked me to stay after class. Instead of criticising me, he went through every mistake with me and showed me that most of them came from the same small misunderstanding. He told me that a mistake is just information about what to practise next. After that, he gave me a small notebook to record my errors, and every week we looked at it together for ten minutes. Within a few months, my marks improved a lot, but more importantly, I stopped being afraid of making mistakes. This was important to me because the same attitude has helped me at university and in my part-time job. Looking back, it was a real turning point in how I see learning.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a friend you enjoy spending time with.
questions.reference: The friend I'd like to describe is Lily, who I've known for about six years. We became friends in our first week of university, when we were put in the same dormitory. On the first night, neither of us could sleep because of the heat, so we ended up sitting on the balcony and talking until three in the morning. We hit it off straight away, because we have a lot in common, like our love of old films and street food. Nowadays we live in different parts of the city, but we still hang out almost every weekend. Usually we explore a new neighbourhood, try a small restaurant, and then go to a cinema that shows classic movies. I enjoy spending time with her for a few reasons. First, she has a great sense of humour, so even ordinary things become funny when she's around. Second, she's very honest. When I'm about to make a bad decision, she tells me directly, but in a kind way. With her, I never feel I have to pretend, and that's rare.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a person you know who is very good at their job.
questions.reference: I'm going to talk about my aunt, who works as a nurse in the emergency department of a hospital in my hometown. I know she's very good at her job from both what other people say and what I've seen myself. A couple of years ago my grandfather had a bad fall and was taken to her hospital late at night. Even though the department was extremely busy, she stayed completely calm. She explained every step to my family in simple language, checked on my grandfather every hour, and noticed a small change in his breathing that the machines hadn't flagged yet. The doctor later told us that her quick reaction probably prevented a much more serious problem. Her colleagues also often ask her for advice, and she's been chosen to train new nurses for three years in a row. How do I feel about her? I really admire her, not just because she's skilled, but because she treats every patient as if they were her own family. She's the reason I believe that attention to detail and kindness can make a huge difference in any job.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe someone older than you whom you admire.
questions.reference: I'd like to describe my neighbour, Mr Wang, who is in his seventies and lives in the flat below mine. I got to know him when I first moved into the building, because he helped me carry my boxes up the stairs, even though he was much older than me. Since then we've chatted almost every day in the courtyard. He's the kind of person who is always curious. At the age of seventy, he decided to learn how to use a smartphone properly, and now he takes photos of the flowers he grows and shares them in a group chat with other residents. He's also very generous with his time. He teaches children in the neighbourhood how to play Chinese chess for free, and he organises a small clean-up every month. What I admire most is his attitude to life. He lost his wife a few years ago, and he could easily have become lonely and bitter, but instead he chose to stay active and help others. He sets a great example for me, because he shows that it's never too late to learn and connect with people.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a place where you go to clear your mind.
questions.reference: The place I'd like to talk about is a small riverside path about fifteen minutes' walk from my apartment. It's on the edge of a park, and most people don't know about it, so it's usually very quiet. I go there about twice a week, especially when I've had a stressful day at school or I need to make a decision. What I do there is really simple. I walk slowly along the river for about half an hour, and then I sit on an old wooden bench under a willow tree. Sometimes I listen to calm music, but more often I just watch the water and the birds. In the evening you can see the lights of the city reflected on the river, which is really beautiful. I think this place helps me clear my mind for two reasons. First, it's one of the few places near my home where I can't hear traffic, so it feels like a world away from my busy life. Second, walking gives my thoughts time to settle, so by the time I go home, problems that seemed huge usually feel much more manageable.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a city or town you visited that you would like to visit again.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about Dali, a city in Yunnan province in south-west China. I went there two summers ago with my cousin, just after my university entrance exam, and we stayed for five days. Dali has an old town with stone streets and traditional houses, and behind it there are mountains, while in front of it there's a huge lake called Erhai. We spent most of our time cycling around the lake, stopping in small villages to take photos and try local food, like grilled cheese and rice noodles. One evening we climbed up to a viewpoint and watched the sunset over the lake, which is still one of the most beautiful things I've ever seen. I'd love to visit it again for a couple of reasons. The main one is that we didn't have enough time. It rained for two days, so we couldn't hike in the mountains as we had planned. Also, the pace of life there is so relaxed that I'd like to stay longer, maybe for two weeks, and just live like a local. Next time, I'd like to bring my parents, because I think they'd love the scenery as much as I did.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a public place in your city that you often go to.
questions.reference: The public place I go to most often is the new city library, which is located in the cultural district, right next to the museum. It opened about three years ago, and the building itself is quite striking. It's shaped like a stack of books, with huge glass windows, so the inside is filled with natural light. There are five floors, including a children's area, a quiet reading room and a café on the ground floor. I usually go there on Saturday mornings and stay for three or four hours. Most of the time I study for my exams in the quiet room, but I also like browsing the new arrivals section, and sometimes I attend free talks about history or photography. I often go there for a few reasons. First, it's a much better place to concentrate than my home, where there are always distractions. Second, it's completely free and open to everyone, which I think is great. And finally, I simply enjoy the atmosphere. Seeing so many people reading quietly motivates me. It's become a kind of second home for me.
questions.goal: 围绕地点、外观、活动与常去原因组织一段连贯陈述

questions.question: Describe a building you find interesting.
questions.reference: The building I find interesting is an old factory in my hometown that has been converted into an arts centre. It's located near the railway station, in an area that used to be full of textile factories. It was originally built in the 1950s, so from the outside it looks quite plain, with red brick walls, tall chimneys and rows of small windows. However, when you go inside, it's a completely different world. The designers kept the old steel beams and some of the machines, but they added glass walls, modern lighting and wooden floors. Nowadays it's used for art exhibitions, small concerts and weekend markets, where local designers sell handmade products. I find it interesting mainly because it combines the city's history with its present. My grandparents actually worked in factories like this one, so when I walk around, I feel connected to their generation. At the same time, it shows that old buildings don't have to be knocked down. They can be given a new life. I think that's a smart and sustainable way to develop a city.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe an object that you use every day and find useful.
questions.reference: The object I'd like to talk about is a stainless steel water bottle. It's nothing special to look at. It's dark blue, about the size of a can, and it has a few scratches on it now. I got it about two years ago as a present from my sister when I started my internship, because she knew I often forgot to drink water when I was busy. I use it every single day. In the morning I fill it with hot tea before I leave home, and it keeps the tea warm until the afternoon. At work, I refill it with water, and I carry it around in my backpack wherever I go. I find it useful for several reasons. First, it's really practical. It keeps drinks hot or cold for hours, and it doesn't leak. Second, it has saved me a lot of money, because I no longer buy bottled drinks. And third, it's better for the environment, since I've probably avoided hundreds of plastic bottles. It's a simple thing, but I honestly can't do without it.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a gift you gave to someone that made them happy.
questions.reference: I'd like to describe a photo album I made for my grandmother's eightieth birthday last year. The idea came to me when I was helping her tidy her room and found a box of old black-and-white photos that were fading and mixed up. I chose this gift because she already has everything she needs, and I wanted to give her something meaningful rather than expensive. So for about a month, I secretly borrowed the photos, scanned them, and asked my parents and aunts to tell me the stories behind them. Then I printed them and put them in a big album in time order, with short notes under each picture, like the year and the people in it. I also added some recent photos of her grandchildren at the end. When I gave it to her at the birthday dinner, her eyes lit up. She turned the pages very slowly and kept telling everyone stories that even my parents had never heard. She was so touched that she cried a little. Now she keeps it on the table next to her bed and shows it to every visitor. For me, it was the best gift I've ever given.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe something you own that you would like to replace.
questions.reference: Something I'd really like to replace is my laptop. I've had it for about five years now. My parents bought it for me when I started university, and at that time it was quite a good model. It has been with me through all my assignments and my graduation thesis, so I'm a bit attached to it. However, it has started to cause a lot of problems. The battery only lasts about forty minutes, so I always have to sit near a socket. It has also slowed down a lot. Opening a large file or joining a video call can take several minutes, and the fan makes a loud noise, which is embarrassing in the library. A couple of keys don't work properly either. I would like to replace it with a lighter laptop that has a long battery life, because I often work in cafés and on trains. I don't need the most powerful model, but I'd like one with a good screen, since I spend so many hours reading. I'm saving up at the moment, and I hope to buy one before the end of the year.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a piece of clothing that is special to you.
questions.reference: The piece of clothing I'd like to describe is a thick grey scarf that my mother knitted for me. It's quite long, with a simple pattern of dark red stripes at both ends, and it's made of soft wool. She made it for me the winter before I left home to study in northern China, because she was worried I wouldn't be used to the cold. I remember she stayed up late for several weeks to finish it, even though she was busy with work. I wear it almost every day in winter, especially on windy days when I'm cycling to class. I also wear it whenever I travel, because it's big enough to use as a small blanket on trains. It's special to me for two reasons. Firstly, it's handmade, so there's no other scarf exactly like it in the world. Secondly, and more importantly, it has great sentimental value. When I was homesick during my first year, wearing it made me feel as if my mother was close to me. Even though it's a bit worn now, I would never throw it away.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a time when you learned something new outside school.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about the time I learned how to cook properly. It happened three years ago, during the long summer holiday after my first year at university. My parents were both working late that summer, so I decided to take responsibility for dinner. The problem was that I could only make instant noodles. So I learned mainly by watching online tutorials and by asking my grandmother for advice on the phone. At first, it was a disaster. I kept burning the garlic, I put too much salt in everything, and once I even set off the smoke alarm. But I wrote down what went wrong each time, and after a lot of trial and error, I started to get better. By the end of the summer, I could cook about ten dishes, including my grandmother's braised pork, which is quite difficult. I felt really proud of myself. It was the first time I had learned a practical skill completely on my own, without a teacher or an exam. It also made me appreciate how much effort my parents had put into cooking for me all those years.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a time when you had to wait for something important.
questions.reference: I'd like to describe the time I had to wait for my university entrance exam results. The exam was in early June, but the results weren't published until the end of the month, so I had to wait for almost three weeks. This was really important for me, because the score would decide which university I could apply to. During the first few days, I tried not to think about it and spent time with friends, playing basketball and watching films. But as the date got closer, I became more and more anxious. I kept going over the exam questions in my head, trying to work out my score. To distract myself, I started volunteering at a local library, helping to organise books for the summer reading programme, which actually helped a lot. Honestly, the wait felt endless, and I didn't sleep well in the last few nights. When the results finally came out, I was checking the website at midnight with my parents beside me. My score was slightly better than I expected, and I felt a huge sense of relief. Looking back, the waiting was almost harder than the exam itself.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a time when you helped someone solve a problem.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about a time last winter when I helped an elderly man in my neighbourhood. I noticed him standing in front of the self-service machine at the hospital near my home, looking very confused. When I asked if he needed help, he told me he had come to collect his medical test results, but the machine required a phone app and a scan code, and he didn't have a smartphone. He had already been trying for twenty minutes and was worried he'd have to come back another day. So first, I found a staff member and explained the situation. She showed us a service desk where older people could get results without the app, but there was a long queue. I waited with him and chatted to keep him company. When we got to the front, I helped him fill in the paper form, because the print was very small. In the end, he got his results, and he thanked me again and again. I felt really good afterwards, not because I did something difficult, but because it was so simple for me and so hard for him. It made me realise that many older people are being left behind by technology.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a time when you changed your mind about something.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about how I changed my mind about living in a small town. For most of my life, I used to think that small towns were boring and that successful people always moved to big cities. I grew up in a large city myself, and whenever we visited relatives in the countryside, I couldn't wait to go home. My view changed completely two years ago, when I spent a month in a small town in Zhejiang for a university research project. I was expecting to feel bored and isolated, but it turned out to be one of the best months of my life. People there had much more time for each other. My host family invited me to dinner with their neighbours almost every evening, and I noticed that everyone knew each other's names. I also discovered that there were small businesses and young people who had moved back from cities to start online shops and cafés. So I realised my original opinion was based on assumptions, not experience. I felt a bit embarrassed at first, but mostly I felt grateful. It taught me to keep an open mind before judging a place or a group of people.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe an activity you do to stay healthy.
questions.reference: The activity I'd like to describe is swimming, which I've been doing regularly for about two years. I usually go to a public swimming pool near my office three times a week, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday evenings, and I swim for about forty-five minutes each time. Most of the time I go with a colleague, who is also trying to get fitter, so we encourage each other. If one of us feels lazy, the other one sends a message saying, 'See you at the pool.' It really works. Swimming helps me stay healthy in several ways. Physically, it's a full-body workout, but it's gentle on my joints, which is important because I hurt my knee playing football a few years ago. My stamina has improved a lot. At the beginning I could only swim four lengths without stopping, but now I can easily do twenty. Mentally, it's also great. When I'm in the water, I can't look at my phone, so it's the only time in my day when I'm completely disconnected. I've noticed that I sleep much better on the days when I swim.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe a hobby you would like to take up in the future.
questions.reference: A hobby I'd really like to take up in the future is pottery, which means making bowls, cups and plates from clay. I first came across it about a year ago when a friend invited me to a one-day workshop at a small studio downtown. I made a very uneven little cup, but I loved the experience. I've also watched lots of videos online, and it looks very relaxing. To start it properly, I would need to sign up for a regular course, because it's really hard to learn the pottery wheel on your own. The studio offers an eight-week beginner course on weekday evenings, and it includes the clay and the use of the kiln, so I wouldn't need to buy much equipment at first. The main thing I'd need is time. I'd like to take it up for a few reasons. Most of my work is done on a computer, so I'd love to do something hands-on and creative. It would also give me a chance to slow down, since you can't rush clay. And honestly, I like the idea of drinking tea from a cup I made myself.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe an outdoor activity you did with other people.
questions.reference: I'd like to talk about a hiking trip I did last spring with five classmates. We went to a mountain area about two hours by bus from our city. It's quite famous for its bamboo forests and waterfalls, but it's not too crowded if you go early. We started at seven in the morning, carrying backpacks with snacks, water and raincoats. The trail was steep in some places, with stone steps that seemed never-ending. Halfway up, it suddenly started raining heavily, and we had to shelter under a small wooden pavilion for almost an hour. At first, everyone was a bit annoyed, but then someone started telling ghost stories, and we ended up laughing so much that we forgot about the rain. When we finally reached the top in the afternoon, the clouds cleared, and we could see the whole valley. Did I enjoy it? Absolutely. Physically it was exhausting, and my legs hurt for two days afterwards. But what made it special was the teamwork. We waited for the slowest person, shared our food, and helped each other on the slippery parts. It made our friendship much closer.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: Describe an activity that you enjoyed doing as a child.
questions.reference: When I was a child, one activity I really enjoyed was flying kites with my grandfather. I was about seven or eight at the time, and my family lived near a big square next to a river. Every Sunday afternoon in spring, when the wind was strong, my grandfather would take me there. He actually made most of our kites himself, using bamboo sticks and colourful paper, and one of them was shaped like a huge butterfly. We would spend hours on the square, along with lots of other families. My grandfather taught me how to run against the wind to get the kite into the air, and then how to slowly let out the string so it could climb higher and higher. Sometimes our kite got caught in a tree, and we had to wait for the wind to blow it free. I enjoyed it for several reasons. It was one of the few times I could run around freely outside, instead of doing homework. I also loved the feeling of controlling something so high in the sky. But most of all, it was special time with my grandfather, and it still brings back very happy memories.
questions.goal: 围绕任务卡完整、连贯地讲述

questions.question: What qualities make someone a good teacher?
questions.reference: In my view, the most important quality is patience. Students learn at different speeds, and a good teacher can explain the same idea in several ways without making anyone feel stupid. Another key quality is the ability to inspire curiosity. For instance, my best teachers connected lessons to real life, so we wanted to find out more on our own. Of course, subject knowledge matters, but without these personal qualities, even a very knowledgeable teacher may struggle to help students learn.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think people learn more from their family or from school?
questions.reference: It depends on what kind of learning we mean. Schools are clearly better at teaching academic knowledge, like maths or history, because teachers are trained and there's a systematic curriculum. Families, on the other hand, teach values and habits, such as honesty or how to treat other people, mostly by example. On balance, I'd say family has a deeper influence, because children spend their earliest and most formative years at home, and those lessons usually last a lifetime.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has technology changed the way people learn new skills?
questions.reference: The biggest change is that learning has become much more accessible. Nowadays, anyone with a phone can watch free tutorials on almost anything, from cooking to coding, and learn at their own pace. My uncle, for example, learned to repair his own bike entirely from online videos. However, one drawback is the lack of feedback. Without a teacher watching you, it's easy to develop bad habits and not even realise it, so for complex skills, I think some face-to-face guidance is still necessary.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do some friendships last longer than others?
questions.reference: I think the key factor is shared values rather than shared activities. Friendships based only on convenience, like being in the same class, tend to fade when circumstances change. In contrast, if two people trust each other and see the world in a similar way, they can stay close even when they live in different cities. Effort also matters. Long friendships usually survive because both people keep in touch, even with a short message now and then.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has social media affected the way people make friends?
questions.reference: On the positive side, social media makes it much easier to meet people with the same interests, even if they live on the other side of the world. I have a few friends I first met in an online photography group. On the downside, many online connections are quite superficial. People might have hundreds of contacts but very few they could call in a crisis. Overall, I think social media has made friendships wider but not necessarily deeper.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it better to have a few close friends or many friends?
questions.reference: Personally, I believe quality matters more than quantity. Close friends are the ones who support you when things go wrong, and you can be completely honest with them. You simply don't have the time or energy to be that close to dozens of people. That said, having a wide network of acquaintances can be useful, especially for finding jobs or information. So ideally, I'd say a few close friends plus a larger circle of casual friends is the best balance.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What makes a person successful at work?
questions.reference: I'd say there are two main factors. The first is reliability. Employers value people who meet deadlines and do what they promise, even if they aren't the most brilliant in the team. Equally important is the ability to communicate well. Most jobs now involve teamwork, so someone who can explain their ideas clearly and listen to others will usually progress faster. People who also keep learning and adapt to change tend to be the most successful in the long run.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Should people choose a job they love or a job that pays well?
questions.reference: Ideally, people should find a job that combines both, but in reality it's often a trade-off. I think as long as a job pays enough to cover basic needs, it's better to choose something you enjoy. People who hate their work are more likely to burn out, and that affects their health and relationships. On the other hand, for someone supporting a family, a well-paid job might be the responsible choice, at least for a period of time.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think it is important for people to keep learning after they start working?
questions.reference: Absolutely, especially nowadays. Technology is changing so fast that skills can become outdated within a few years. Take accounting as an example. A lot of basic tasks are now automated, so accountants need to learn data analysis to stay useful. Continuous learning is also good for career development, because people who pick up new skills are more likely to be promoted. And personally, I think it keeps work interesting, rather than doing the same thing for thirty years.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What can young people learn from older people?
questions.reference: Quite a lot, actually. Older people have been through many ups and downs, so they often have a calmer perspective on problems that seem huge to young people. My grandmother, for example, always reminds me that most worries disappear with time. They can also teach practical and traditional skills, like cooking family recipes or repairing things, which are slowly being lost. I think spending time with older people helps young people become more patient and grounded.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has the role of grandparents changed in modern families?
questions.reference: In the past, grandparents were mainly seen as the heads of the family, and their opinions on major decisions carried a lot of weight. Nowadays, in many Chinese cities, their role has become much more practical. Because both parents usually work full-time, grandparents often take care of young children every day, cooking and picking them up from school. At the same time, they have less authority than before, since young parents prefer to make their own decisions about things like education.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What problems do elderly people face in modern cities?
questions.reference: One major problem is the rapid shift to digital services. Things like booking a doctor's appointment or paying for parking increasingly require a smartphone, and many elderly people feel left behind. Another issue is loneliness. Their children often work long hours or live in other cities, so they may spend most of the day alone. As a result, many elderly people feel isolated, even though they live surrounded by millions of people.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How can cities provide better spaces for people to relax?
questions.reference: One practical solution would be to create more small pocket parks in residential areas, rather than just one huge park on the edge of the city. That way, people could relax for ten minutes without travelling far. Cities could also turn some busy streets into pedestrian areas at weekends, with benches, trees and space for street performers. This would allow people to slow down and enjoy the city, and it could also help local shops.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do many people find it hard to relax nowadays?
questions.reference: I think there are a couple of reasons. First of all, work pressure has increased. In many companies, there's strong competition, and people worry about losing their jobs, so they keep thinking about work even at home. On top of that, smartphones mean we're always connected. Your boss can send you a message at eleven at night, and even in your free time you're scrolling through endless information. This makes it very difficult to switch off completely.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think people need quiet places more than they did in the past?
questions.reference: Yes, I'd say so. Compared with the past, most people now live in crowded cities with constant traffic, construction and advertising screens. Even at home, we're surrounded by notifications. As a result, our brains are overstimulated almost all day. Quiet places, like libraries, temples or parks, give us a chance to concentrate and recover mentally. In the past, when life was slower and more people lived in the countryside, quiet was simply part of daily life, so people didn't need to look for it.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What makes a city attractive to tourists?
questions.reference: I think the most important thing is having something unique, whether that's historic sites, special food or a distinctive culture. A good example is Xi'an, which attracts visitors because of the Terracotta Warriors and its famous street food. Practical things also matter, though. A city with convenient public transport, clean streets and clear signs in English is much easier to enjoy. And friendly locals can make a huge difference to a tourist's impression.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How does tourism affect local people?
questions.reference: It has both positive and negative effects. On the one hand, tourism creates jobs in hotels, restaurants and shops, and it can encourage people to preserve local traditions. On the other hand, it can push up living costs. In some popular old towns, rents have risen so much that local families have moved out, and the streets are full of souvenir shops instead of normal businesses. The key is managing tourist numbers so that local people also benefit.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think travelling to other cities is a good way to learn?
questions.reference: Definitely. Travel gives you first-hand experience of how other people live, which is very different from reading about it. For instance, when I visited Guangzhou, I learned a lot about Cantonese culture just by eating dim sum with locals and hearing the dialect in the streets. Travel also makes people more open-minded, because you realise your own way of doing things isn't the only way. That said, you need to be curious and talk to people, not just take photos.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why are public places like libraries and parks important for a community?
questions.reference: First, they give everyone equal access to resources, regardless of income. A student who can't afford books or a quiet room at home can study in a library for free, and a family without a garden can enjoy a park. Second, they bring people together. In parks, you see neighbours chatting, children playing and older people dancing, which builds a sense of community. Without these places, people would spend more time alone at home, and cities would feel much colder.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How have public places in cities changed in recent years?
questions.reference: They've changed quite a lot. In my city, many old parks have been renovated with running tracks, better lighting and fitness equipment, so they're busy until late at night. Another trend is that public places have become more multi-functional. Libraries now host talks, exhibitions and even coding classes for kids, rather than just lending books. Technology has also been added. You can reserve a study seat with your phone, and some parks have smart screens showing air quality.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Who should be responsible for keeping public places clean?
questions.reference: I think it's a shared responsibility. The local government should provide enough bins, employ cleaners and make sure rubbish is collected regularly. However, no matter how many cleaners there are, places will stay dirty if people keep throwing litter on the ground. So at the same time, individuals need to take responsibility for their own rubbish. Education plays a big role here. If children learn from a young age to take their rubbish home, they'll probably keep that habit as adults.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Should old buildings be protected or replaced with new ones?
questions.reference: It depends on the building. Buildings with real historical or cultural value should definitely be protected, because once they're knocked down, they can never be replaced, and they give a city its character. However, not every old building is special. If a building is unsafe or can't meet modern needs, like old apartments without lifts, it might be better to rebuild. So I think cities need clear rules to decide which buildings are worth saving.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What makes a building beautiful?
questions.reference: For me, a beautiful building is one that fits in with its surroundings. A glass skyscraper might look great in a financial district but completely wrong next to a historic temple. It also depends on materials and light. Buildings that use natural materials like wood and stone, and let in plenty of natural light, feel warm and welcoming. A good example would be some of the new libraries in China, which are modern but designed around courtyards, like traditional houses.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How do you think homes will change in the future?
questions.reference: I think homes will become much smarter and more energy-efficient. It's likely that lights, heating and appliances will adjust automatically to save electricity, and solar panels will be common even on apartment buildings. Also, because more people now work from home at least part of the time, homes might be designed with more flexible spaces, for example a room that can be an office during the day and a guest room at night.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What everyday objects have changed people's lives the most?
questions.reference: The obvious answer is the smartphone. It has completely changed the way we communicate, shop, pay and even find our way around. But I'd also mention the washing machine, which people often forget. Before it became common, washing clothes by hand took hours every week, and this work was mostly done by women. So the washing machine gave many people, especially women, much more time for work, study or rest.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do people buy things they don't really need?
questions.reference: There are several reasons. One is clever marketing. Online platforms constantly offer discounts and limited-time deals, which make people feel they'll lose out if they don't buy immediately. Another reason is that shopping can be emotional. Some people shop to cheer themselves up after a stressful day, which is often called retail therapy. Social pressure also plays a part. When everyone around you has the latest gadget, it's tempting to buy one too, even if your old one works perfectly well.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it better to buy cheap things or expensive, high-quality things?
questions.reference: For things we use every day, like shoes, a mattress or a laptop, I think it's worth paying more for high quality, because they last longer and are more comfortable. In the long run, buying one good pair of shoes can be cheaper than buying three cheap pairs that fall apart. However, for items we rarely use or that go out of fashion quickly, cheaper options make more sense. So it's really about value for money, not just the price.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do people give gifts?
questions.reference: People give gifts for many reasons, but mainly it's a way to show that they care about someone. On birthdays or festivals, a gift says, 'I remember you and I value our relationship.' Gifts are also used to say thank you, for example to a teacher or a colleague who helped you. In China, there's also a tradition of bringing a small gift when visiting someone's home, like fruit or tea, as a sign of respect and good manners.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is the price of a gift important?
questions.reference: Generally speaking, I don't think so. What matters more is how much thought goes into the gift. A cheap book that matches someone's interests can mean much more than an expensive perfume they'll never use. In some situations, though, price does matter. In business or at weddings in China, for example, the value of a gift can be seen as a sign of respect, and giving something too cheap might cause embarrassment. So it depends on the context.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has online shopping changed the way people give gifts?
questions.reference: It has made gift-giving much more convenient. You can now choose from millions of products and have them delivered directly to someone in another city, even on the same day. This is great for people who live far from their families. The downside is that gifts can feel less personal. It only takes a few clicks, so some people choose something at the last minute without much thought, and the recipient might sense that. Personally, I still prefer to add a handwritten card.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do people replace things that still work?
questions.reference: I think it's partly about image. For many young people, having the latest phone is a kind of status symbol, so they upgrade every year even if their old phone works fine. Companies also encourage this by releasing new models constantly and advertising small improvements as huge changes. In some cases, older devices stop receiving software updates, so apps run slowly. As a result, people feel they have no choice but to replace them.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it better to repair things or to buy new ones?
questions.reference: Where possible, I think repairing is better. It reduces waste, and it's often cheaper. Replacing a phone battery, for example, costs much less than a new phone. It also helps small local repair shops stay in business. However, sometimes repairing isn't realistic. Spare parts can be hard to find for older products, or the repair might cost almost as much as a new item. In those cases, buying new and recycling the old one properly may be the sensible choice.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How can people be encouraged to produce less waste?
questions.reference: One effective way is to use money. For example, charging a small fee for plastic bags has greatly reduced their use in many countries, because people start bringing their own bags. Businesses can also help by using less packaging, especially for online deliveries, where a small item often comes in a huge box. Finally, making recycling simple is important. If bins are clearly labelled and collected regularly, people are much more willing to sort their rubbish.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do people care about what they wear?
questions.reference: Clothes are one of the first things people notice about us, so they strongly affect first impressions. For example, in a job interview, dressing smartly shows that you take the opportunity seriously. Clothes also affect how we feel about ourselves. Many people feel more confident when they wear something they like. And for young people especially, clothes are a way to express their identity or to fit in with a group of friends.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has fashion changed in your country in recent years?
questions.reference: One noticeable trend is the return of traditional Chinese elements. Young people now wear clothes inspired by traditional styles, like Hanfu, not only at festivals but sometimes in everyday life. Another change is that domestic brands have become much more popular. In the past, many people preferred foreign brands, but now Chinese brands are seen as stylish and good quality. This is partly because of national pride and partly because of influencers who promote these brands on social media.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think people judge others by their appearance too much?
questions.reference: Unfortunately, I think they do. It's natural to form a quick impression, but many people then stick to it without getting to know the person. Social media has made this worse, because people see thousands of edited photos and start to believe everyone should look perfect. This can be unfair to people who don't fit those standards, for example in job interviews or dating. I think we need more awareness that appearance tells us very little about someone's ability or character.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What are the benefits of learning things outside school?
questions.reference: The main benefit is that people learn practical, real-world skills that schools often don't teach, such as cooking, managing money or repairing things. Another advantage is motivation. When you learn something outside school, it's usually because you're genuinely interested, not because of an exam, so you tend to enjoy it more and remember it better. For example, many teenagers who learn video editing for fun end up being very skilled at it, simply because they chose it themselves.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do some people stop learning after they finish school?
questions.reference: One reason is simply lack of time. Once people start working and have families, their free time is limited, and learning feels like a luxury. Another reason might be the way they experienced school. If education was all about exams and pressure, people may feel burnt out and associate learning with stress, so they avoid it later. For some people, there's also no clear reward. If their job doesn't require new skills, they don't see the point of continuing to study.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is learning from experience better than learning from books?
questions.reference: Both have their strengths. Learning from experience is often more memorable, because you feel the consequences directly. If you get lost in a new city once, you remember the route forever. Books, on the other hand, let you learn from other people's experiences without making every mistake yourself, and they explain the theory behind things. A doctor, for example, needs both years of study and hands-on practice. So ideally, the two should go together rather than compete.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why are people less patient nowadays?
questions.reference: I think it's mainly because we're used to getting things instantly. These days, food can be delivered in thirty minutes, films are available on demand, and we get answers to any question in seconds online. So when something takes longer, like waiting in a queue or waiting for a reply, it feels unbearable. The fast pace of city life also plays a role. People have busy schedules, so any delay feels like a waste of their limited time.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: In what situations is it important to be patient?
questions.reference: One obvious situation is when you're learning something difficult, like a foreign language or a musical instrument. Progress is slow, and if you're impatient, you'll probably give up too early. Patience is also essential when dealing with people, especially children or elderly relatives. They may need things explained several times, and losing your temper only makes things worse. Otherwise, relationships can be damaged by moments of frustration that we later regret.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How do businesses try to reduce waiting times for customers?
questions.reference: Many businesses now use technology. For instance, in restaurants you can scan a code and order from your phone, so you don't have to wait for a waiter. Hospitals and banks let people book appointments online, which reduces crowds. Another common method is self-service machines, like in supermarkets and train stations. Some businesses also try to make waiting feel shorter, for example by giving customers a queue number and free snacks, so they can relax instead of standing in line.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do some people enjoy helping others?
questions.reference: For many people, helping others gives them a sense of purpose and makes them feel good about themselves. When you see that you've made someone's day easier, it's very satisfying. It also depends on their upbringing. People who grew up seeing their parents help neighbours are more likely to do the same. And some people simply have strong empathy. They can easily imagine how others feel, so they naturally want to help when they see someone struggling.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it better to solve problems alone or with other people?
questions.reference: It depends on the type of problem. For complex problems, working with others is usually better, because different people bring different knowledge and perspectives, and they can spot mistakes you might miss. In my group projects at university, the best ideas often came from discussion. But for simple or very personal problems, solving them alone can be faster and more comfortable. Group discussions can take a lot of time, and sometimes too many opinions make it harder to decide.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What role should volunteers play in society?
questions.reference: I think volunteers play an important supporting role. They can fill gaps where public services don't reach, for example visiting lonely elderly people or helping at community events. During emergencies like floods, volunteers often arrive quickly and provide practical help. Volunteering also builds community spirit, because people from different backgrounds work together. However, they shouldn't replace trained professionals or government responsibility. Important services like healthcare need stable funding and qualified staff, not just goodwill.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do people sometimes change their opinions?
questions.reference: The most common reason is new information. When people learn facts they didn't know before, a reasonable person adjusts their view. Personal experience can also change opinions very strongly. Someone might think a job is easy until they actually try it. As people get older, their priorities shift too. For example, many young people don't care much about saving money, but once they have children, they often change their minds completely.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How do people usually make important decisions?
questions.reference: Most people start by collecting information and weighing up the pros and cons. For example, when choosing a university, they compare rankings, locations and costs. They also tend to consult people they trust, like parents, teachers or friends who have been in a similar situation. In the end, though, I think many important decisions come down to gut feeling. Even after all the research, people often choose the option that simply feels right.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it easy to persuade people to change their habits?
questions.reference: Not at all, in my experience. Habits are hard to break because they're automatic. People don't even think about them, and changing them means leaving their comfort zone. Simply telling someone that a habit is bad, like eating too much sugar, rarely works. What tends to work better is showing clear personal benefits and suggesting small steps. For instance, my father only started exercising when his doctor showed him his test results and suggested a short walk after dinner.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do some people find it difficult to live a healthy lifestyle?
questions.reference: The biggest obstacle is probably time. Many people work long hours and commute for an hour or more, so by the time they get home, they're too tired to cook or exercise. Another problem is that unhealthy options are cheap and convenient. Fast food can be delivered in minutes, while preparing a healthy meal takes planning. So even if people know what they should do, they often choose the easiest option, especially when they're stressed.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Should governments do more to encourage people to exercise?
questions.reference: Yes, I think they should, because public health affects everyone. One thing they could do is build more free or cheap sports facilities, like outdoor courts and cycling paths, especially in crowded neighbourhoods. They could also organise community events, such as city marathons or free fitness classes in parks. In the long run, this would reduce healthcare costs, because people who exercise regularly are less likely to develop serious illnesses. It's an investment rather than an expense.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has people's diet changed in recent years?
questions.reference: There seem to be two opposite trends. On one side, people eat more processed food and takeaway meals than before, because of busy lifestyles and delivery apps. Sugary drinks, especially milk tea, have become hugely popular among young people. On the other side, more people are becoming health-conscious. Supermarkets now sell more organic vegetables and low-sugar products, and many young office workers bring healthy lunches or track their calories with apps. Overall, the gap between healthy and unhealthy eaters seems to be growing.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why is it important for people to have hobbies?
questions.reference: Hobbies give people a break from the pressure of work or study. When you're doing something you love, like painting or playing an instrument, you forget about your worries for a while, which is good for mental health. They also help people meet others with similar interests, so hobbies can expand your social life. Besides, hobbies give people a sense of identity beyond their job. Without hobbies, life can become just a cycle of working, eating and sleeping.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How are the hobbies of young people different from those of older people?
questions.reference: Young people's hobbies tend to be more screen-based, like playing video games, editing videos or following online content creators. Older people, by contrast, often prefer physical and social activities, such as square dancing, practising tai chi in parks or playing cards with neighbours. Interestingly, though, the gap is getting smaller. More older people now enjoy taking photos with their phones and sharing them online, and some young people have become interested in traditional hobbies like calligraphy or tea culture.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do people have enough free time nowadays?
questions.reference: For many people, I'd say no. In big cities, long working hours and overtime are common, and people often spend two hours a day commuting. Also, because of smartphones, the boundary between work and free time has become blurred. People answer work messages in the evening and at weekends. It varies, though. Retired people and some students may have plenty of free time. But for working adults, especially parents with young children, real free time is quite rare.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Why do many people prefer indoor activities nowadays?
questions.reference: One reason is that home entertainment has become so attractive. With streaming services, video games and food delivery, people can have a great time without leaving the sofa. In addition, many people live in cities where there isn't much green space nearby, so going outdoors requires planning and travel. Weather and pollution also play a part. On very hot or smoggy days, staying in an air-conditioned room is simply more comfortable. It's a matter of convenience more than choice.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: What are the benefits of doing activities in a group?
questions.reference: The first benefit is motivation. When you exercise or study with a group, you're less likely to give up, because others are expecting you to show up. Group activities also teach social skills like cooperation and communication. On a team hike, for example, you have to agree on the pace and look after each other. Not to mention that they're simply more fun. Sharing an experience with others makes it more memorable, and it's a great way to make new friends.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Should schools organise more outdoor activities for students?
questions.reference: Yes, definitely. Students spend most of their day sitting in classrooms and then doing homework, so they get very little fresh air or exercise. Outdoor activities are good for their physical and mental health. They also allow hands-on learning. A biology lesson in a forest or a history trip to an old town is much more memorable than a textbook. Of course, safety needs to be carefully planned, but that shouldn't be a reason to keep students indoors all the time.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: How has the way children play changed over the years?
questions.reference: In the past, children usually played outside with other kids in the neighbourhood, inventing their own games with very simple things like stones or skipping ropes. These days, a lot of play happens on digital devices, like tablets and game consoles. Children's free time is also more organised. Many attend classes in drawing, music or sports at weekends. One reason for this change is that parents worry more about safety, so they prefer children to play at home or in supervised activities.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Do you think children today are under too much pressure?
questions.reference: Yes, I'm afraid many of them are. In China, the competition starts very early. Some children attend after-school classes almost every day, even in primary school, because parents worry they'll fall behind. The pressure to get into a good school is intense. As a consequence, some children suffer from anxiety or lack of sleep, and they don't have enough time to simply play and be children. Recently, there have been policies to reduce homework, which I think is a positive step.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑

questions.question: Is it important for children to play with other children?
questions.reference: Yes, it's extremely important. Through playing together, children learn to share, take turns and deal with conflict, which are skills they'll need for the rest of their lives. For example, when two kids want the same toy, they have to negotiate or find a compromise. These skills are hard to learn from adults or screens, because adults usually give way to children, and games on tablets don't involve real people. Playing with others also helps children become more confident and less shy.
questions.goal: 明确观点，并用原因、对比或例子支撑
